Tree Removal Cost Calculator — What It Really Runs in NE Ohio

Removal in Greater Cleveland ranges from about $200 for a small backyard tree to $10,000+ for a crane-assisted estate oak. This calculator walks every factor that decides where inside that range your job lands — size, species, access, permit fees, stump grinding and emergency timing — so you can budget before you call.

Tree removal is the one job where the sticker range feels impossibly wide — $200 to $10,000+. The number is not random. Five inputs explain nearly all of it: tree size, species, site access, your village's permit rules, and whether you add stump grinding. Work through them below, then call for a real number.

How to Estimate in Five Steps

You can put a working budget on almost any tree in about fifteen minutes with these five steps. For a real number on a real tree, call {{global.phone}} — most jobs can be quoted on-site in 15–30 minutes.

  1. Measure tree height. Use the stories of an adjacent house as a rough scale (one story ≈ 10 feet), or the "pencil method" — hold a pencil at arm's length, align it with the tree, then rotate it to the ground.
  2. Estimate trunk diameter (DBH). Diameter at Breast Height is the trunk width at 4.5 feet up. Wrap a string around the trunk at chest height and divide the circumference by 3.14.
  3. Match to a size category. Find your tree in the size matrix below and pick the row for your height and DBH.
  4. Add modifiers. Hardwood vs. softwood, access constraints, crane requirement, your village permit fee, a stump grinding add-on, and emergency timing each add a range to the base price.
  5. Add a 10–15% buffer. Real jobs surface real surprises — soft soil, hidden utilities, a fence not visible in photos. A 10–15% buffer is honest budgeting.

Access — What Shifts the Base Price

After size, access is the single biggest lever on the final number. A tree a bucket truck can stage next to prices very differently from the same tree tucked behind a house or a six-foot gate.

Access situationEffect on price
Wide driveway, open accessStandard pricing — bucket truck can stage close
Narrow driveway / 6 ft gate+10–20% — climbing job; smaller equipment
Adjacent power lines (non-energized)+15–25% — careful drop-zone management
Adjacent energized power linesUtility coordination required first; cost varies — Roubic will not touch energized lines without utility clearance
Tight to house / pool / fence+20–40% — rigging required; extra time to lower limbs safely
Soft lawn / wet ground+5–15% — driveway protection (plywood mats); slower equipment cycles
Crane access required+$500–$2,500+ — Roubic in-house crane (no subcontract markup)
Multi-tree job (same property)−5–15% per tree — staging cost amortized; package pricing

Species — the Hardwood Premium

Hardwoods like oak, hickory, beech and sugar maple take longer to cut and chip than softwoods like pine, willow and poplar. The denser the wood, the more time on the saw and the more wear on the chipper. Expect a 10–20% premium on the base price for dense hardwoods. Roubic's crew is set up for both — professional-grade chainsaws and a chipper rated for hardwood limbs.

Permit Fees by Village

Several Greater Cleveland villages have tree-protection ordinances requiring a permit to remove a healthy tree above a set DBH. Hazard trees (dead or dying) usually follow an expedited review. Roubic routinely coordinates the permit workflow as part of the removal job — we know the contact, the form and the typical review timeline for each village.

Permit fees and DBH thresholds change occasionally, so verify current rules with the village building department or ask Roubic to confirm during the estimate. We carry the permit conversation on every job that needs one.

Stump Grinding Add-on

Most removal customers add stump grinding to the same visit. Bundled pricing typically runs $150–$500 per stump depending on diameter and access — lower than the standalone rate because the crew and equipment are already on-site. Skipping the grind saves money short-term but leaves a tripping hazard, a re-sprout source for maple, elm and willow, and a target for carpenter ants and termites within two to three years. See the Stump Grinding service page for full grinding-specific pricing.

When Homeowners Insurance Covers Removal

Homeowners insurance typically covers tree removal in three scenarios: a tree fell and damaged a covered structure (house, garage, some fences, a vehicle in covered cases); a tree fell in a covered storm event and is blocking essential access; or a qualified arborist established imminent risk to a covered structure before failure. It does not cover routine removal of a healthy tree, removal of a dead tree that hasn't damaged anything, or aesthetic view-clearing. Storm Damage & Emergency Tree Care is the most insurance-relevant category, and Roubic supplies the documentation adjusters need — photos, itemized work, species and DBH estimates.

Bottom Line — Aaron's Advice

The cheapest quote is rarely the safest. Read the line items, not just the total — a quote with no insurance documentation, no written method and no cleanup scope is hiding something, usually the parts that protect you.

If the estimate feels too low, it's usually because something's excluded — permit filing, chip haul, insurance documentation. Ask what's in the price, not just what the price is. {{global.owner_name}} · Owner

Common Tree Removal Cost Questions

Tree Removal Cost FAQ

How much does it cost to remove a tree in NE Ohio?
Removal in Greater Cleveland typically runs $200–$10,000+ depending on size, species, access and permit requirements. Small trees under 20 ft start at $200–$500; medium trees run $500–$1,500; large trees $1,500–$3,500; and very large trees over 80 ft can exceed $10,000 when a crane is required. See the size matrix above for ranges by category.
How is tree removal cost calculated?
Cost starts from a base price tied to size (height + DBH), plus modifiers for species hardness, access constraints, crane requirement, permit fees, a stump grinding add-on and emergency timing. The base accounts for roughly 60–70% of the typical quote; the modifiers explain the rest of the variance.
Do hardwoods cost more to remove than softwoods?
Yes. Hardwoods like oak, hickory, beech and sugar maple take longer to cut and chip than softwoods like pine, willow and poplar. Expect a 10–20% premium on the base price for dense hardwoods — crew time on the saw and chipper wear are the underlying drivers.
Is tree removal covered by homeowners insurance?
Usually only when a tree damages a covered structure — house, garage, certain fence types, or a vehicle in covered scenarios. Insurance does not cover routine removal of healthy or dead trees that haven't damaged anything. Storm work where a tree fell on the house is generally covered, and Roubic provides the documentation insurers need (photos, itemized work, species and DBH).
How can I lower my tree removal cost?
Three reliable approaches: schedule in winter, when leaves-off access can speed crews up by 10–20%; accept chip-drop on-site instead of full haul-off, saving $50–$150 in disposal; and bundle stump grinding with the removal for the package rate. Size and access generally can't be changed, so be wary of quotes that promise unrealistically low numbers — they often skip safety steps or surprise-bill on add-ons.
